text: Moving a 50-tonne body costs a lot of energy. A long neck let a [[sauropod|sauropod]] reach a huge area of leaves while standing still, sweeping its head up, down and sideways.

The necks were surprisingly light, with air pockets inside the bones, like a bird's. Their heads were tiny. They didn't chew; they stripped leaves and swallowed them whole, and their giant gut did the slow work of breaking them down.

st.prompt: What do you think the long neck was mainly for?
st.reveal: Most scientists think the neck was a food tool. A sauropod could stand still and sweep its head over a huge area, high and low, eating without moving its giant body. Walking costs lots of energy!
st.nudge: Good thinking! It may have helped a little. But the main idea is about food.

d.try: Stand in the middle of a room with a broom held out like a long neck. Without moving your feet, see how much of the floor you can touch with the broom's end. Then try with just your hand. A long neck works like that broom, letting a heavy animal reach food without walking.
myth: Sauropods were too heavy to walk on land, so they lived in lakes and swamps.
Scientists once thought this, more than a hundred years ago. Footprints, leg bones and their deep chests show they walked on dry land, holding up their weight on pillar-like legs, as elephants do.
facts: up to 19 in some kinds (a giraffe has 7)

sec.t:
A crane at a building site doesn't drive around to lift each load. It stays put and swings its arm. Many scientists think a sauropod's neck worked the same way.

Walking, for an animal the weight of ten elephants, burned a great deal of energy. Standing in one spot and sweeping a long neck across trees and ferns was far cheaper. Every mouthful reached without a step was energy saved for growing and staying alive. A sauropod also needed a vast amount of food, so the more ground it could cover from one spot, the better.

A neck 15 metres long, made of solid bone, would have been impossibly heavy. Sauropod neck bones were full of hollow spaces. Air sacs, linked to the lungs, pushed into the bones and left them more like honeycomb than solid stone.

Birds have the same system today. It's one of the many clues linking dinosaurs to [[@birds-dinosaurs|birds]]. Air sacs may also have helped sauropods breathe through such long necks, moving air in one direction through their lungs, as birds do, rather than in and out like [[@lungs-breathe|your lungs]].

A giraffe has seven neck bones, the same number as you or a mouse. [[mammal|Mammals]] almost always have seven, however long the neck. Sauropods had no such limit. Many had 15 or more neck bones, and Mamenchisaurus had 19.

Each bone could also be long, in some giants more than a metre. More bones and longer bones together made those record necks.

Here the scientists disagree. Some think necks were held high, like a giraffe's, to reach treetops other animals couldn't. Others point out that pumping blood up to a head 9 metres above the heart would need a giant, powerful [[@heart-beat|heart]].

Many now think it varied. Brachiosaurus had long front legs and probably reached high. Diplodocus may have swept low over ferns. Either way, the neck let them feed without moving.

India had sauropods too. [[@barapasaurus|Barapasaurus]], from the Godavari valley in Telangana, was one of the early ones, about 18 metres long. Its name means "big-leg lizard".

Later, giant titanosaurs roamed India and laid eggs in Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh. In South America, titanosaurs like [[@argentinosaurus|Argentinosaurus]] may have weighed more than 60 tonnes. Long necks were one part of how sauropods became the biggest animals ever to walk on land.

text: Flamingos are pink because of what they eat. Their food, tiny [[algae|algae]] and small creatures such as brine shrimp, contains [[pigment|pigments]] called carotenoids. These are the same kind of colour chemicals that make carrots orange and [[@tomatoes|tomatoes]] red.

As a flamingo digests its food, its body turns these pigments into pink and red colours, which end up in its new feathers, skin and legs. Flamingos that eat more of them are brighter. Chicks hatch grey and take two or three years to turn fully pink.

st.prompt: Zoo flamingos started turning pale. What did keepers do to bring back their pink?

options.t: Added pink-making pigments to their food

st.reveal: Flamingos get their colour from pigments called carotenoids in their food. Zoos add these pigments to the birds' meals. Without them, new feathers grow in pale.

d.try: Time how long you can stand on one leg with your eyes open. Then try with your eyes closed. Then try it with your knee bent and your other foot tucked up, like a flamingo. Flamingos can sleep standing this way.
myth: Flamingos are born pink.
Flamingo chicks hatch with grey or white fluffy down. They slowly turn pink over two to three years as they eat food rich in carotenoid pigments.

sec.t:
A flamingo feeds with its head upside down. It wades into shallow, often salty water, dips its head and sweeps its bent beak from side to side.

Its tongue works like a pump, sucking water in and pushing it out. The edges of the beak are lined with comb-like plates that act as a strainer. Mud and water flow out. Algae, shrimp and other tiny food stay in. Whales like the [[@blue-whale|blue whale]] feed in a similar way, using plates of baleen.

The lesser flamingo eats mostly tiny blue-green algae and is a deeper pink. The greater flamingo, which is taller and paler, eats more small shrimp, worms and insect [[larva|larvae]].

Every winter, tens of thousands of flamingos gather on the mudflats of Thane Creek in Mumbai, within sight of busy roads and tall buildings. In 2015, part of the creek was declared the Thane Creek Flamingo Sanctuary.

The biggest breeding grounds in India are in the [[@gujarat-rann|Rann of Kutch]] in Gujarat. After good [[monsoon|monsoon]] rains, the salty flats fill with shallow water, and huge colonies of greater flamingos build mud-mound nests there. The place is so famous that it is nicknamed Flamingo City. Flamingos depend on [[@wetlands|wetlands]] like these, which are easily lost to building and pollution.

Flamingos often stand, and even sleep, on one leg. Why they do it has been debated for years. One idea is that tucking a leg into their feathers keeps them warm, since less skin is exposed to cold water.

Another idea comes from a 2017 study in the USA. Researchers found that a flamingo's body can balance on one leg almost without using its muscles, locking into place like a folding stand. Both reasons may be true.

Flamingos are found in Asia, Africa, Europe and the Americas, and there are six [[species|species]] in all. The American flamingo lives in the Caribbean and parts of Florida.

In 1957, an American designer named Don Featherstone created a [[@plastic-made|plastic]] pink flamingo for gardens. Millions have been sold, and the plastic bird is now far more common in American yards than real ones. A group of flamingos, by the way, is called a flamboyance.

text: An airbag is a folded nylon bag hidden in the steering wheel, the dashboard, the seats or the side of the roof. It inflates only in a crash.

Sensors in the car feel for a very sudden slowdown, much sharper than any normal braking. When that happens, a small computer sends an electric signal to a device called an inflator. The signal sets off a quick chemical reaction that produces a large puff of nitrogen gas. The gas rushes into the bag and fills it in about 30 thousandths of a second, faster than a blink.
The bag then starts to empty at once through small holes, so it cushions you instead of bouncing you back.

st.prompt: How long does a front airbag take to fill up in a crash?

options.t: About half a second, like clapping your hands
About the time of one blink

st.reveal: A front airbag fills in roughly 30 thousandths of a second. A blink takes around 100 to 150 thousandths, so the bag is full several times faster than you could close your eyes. Then it starts to empty right away, through small vents.

d.try: Feel how a soft landing helps. Drop a raw potato or a ball onto a hard floor, then onto a thick cushion. Notice the cushion lets it stop more slowly, over a longer distance. An airbag does the same for your head, turning a sudden hard stop into a slower, gentler one.
myth: If a car has airbags, you don't need to wear a seatbelt.

Airbags are designed to work together with seatbelts. Without a belt, a person can slide forward and hit the bag too early or in the wrong place, which can cause serious injuries. Belt first, airbag second.
facts: mostly nitrogen, made by a chemical reaction
Front airbags required in all new US cars

sec.t:
In a crash, the car stops almost instantly, but the people inside keep moving forward. The airbag has to be in place before they reach the steering wheel or dashboard. Human [[@reflexes|reflexes]] are far too slow to help: by the time your brain notices a crash, it is already over. The car has to think for you.

Modern cars use electronic [[sensor|sensors]] called accelerometers, small chips that measure how fast speed is changing. Many smartphones contain the same kind of chip to know which way up they are. The car's computer compares the readings with patterns of real crashes. A bump in the road or a hard stop shouldn't trigger the bag. A crash into a wall at speed should.

Stopping suddenly is what hurts in a crash. An airbag spreads that stop over a slightly longer time and a larger area of your body. Instead of your head hitting a hard wheel, it sinks into a soft, emptying cushion.

But an airbag opens with great force. It is designed for an adult wearing a [[@seatbelts|seatbelt]], which holds the body in the right place. That's why safety agencies in the USA and elsewhere say children under 13 should ride in the back seat. A baby's rear-facing car seat must never go in front of an active airbag.

Inventors in the USA and Germany patented early airbag ideas in the early 1950s, but the technology for fast sensors and safe inflators took decades. Some luxury [[@cars-history|cars]] offered airbags in the 1970s and 1980s.

In the USA, front airbags became compulsory for both front seats in all new cars from 1998. In India, the government made front airbags compulsory in new cars in the early 2020s. Many cars now have six or more airbags, including curtains that drop down beside the windows. Safety rules took years of argument, testing and crash data, and [[@road-safety|road safety]] experts still say the cheapest protection of all is the belt.

text: A light switch is a gate in a loop of wire. Electricity can only flow when the loop, called a [[circuit|circuit]], is complete. When you flip the switch on, two pieces of metal inside press together and close the gap. Electric current flows from the supply, through the bulb and back again, and the bulb lights up.

Flip it off and a spring pulls the metal pieces apart. There's now a tiny air gap. Air doesn't carry electricity well, so the current stops and the room goes dark. Everything else, from the wires in your walls to the [[@electricity-made|power station]] miles away, stays exactly as it was.

st.prompt: The light comes on as soon as you flip the switch. How fast do the electrons in the wire actually move along it?

options.t: About as fast as a car on a highway

st.reveal: The electrons themselves barely move. The wire is already full of them, so when the switch closes, they all start being pushed at once, like water in a full pipe. That push travels almost as fast as light.

d.try: With an adult's help, take a torch apart and find its switch. Watch how sliding it presses two pieces of metal together. Then look at the light switches at home and count how many places can turn the same light on and off.
myth: Switching a light off and on again uses more electricity than leaving it on.
For ordinary bulbs and LEDs, switching off saves electricity, even for a few minutes. The tiny surge when a light starts is far smaller than the energy it would use staying on.
facts: opens or closes a gap in a circuit
two-way switches, one at each end

sec.t:
Open up an ordinary switch (only an electrician should do this) and you find a small seesaw of brass or copper, a spring and two screws where wires attach. Pressing the switch tips the seesaw so its contacts touch.

The spring is there for a reason. It makes the contacts snap together or apart quickly. If they drifted slowly, electricity could jump across the narrowing gap as a spark, which heats and wears the metal. That's why most switches give a firm click.

Indian homes usually have rows of switches on a single board, often with a small red or orange dot that shows which way is on. In India you usually press a switch down to turn a light on, while in the USA you usually flip it up. The plastic case around them doesn't carry electricity, so your finger never touches the metal inside.

Electricians always put the switch on the live wire, the one that carries the push from the supply. When the switch is off, the bulb holder is cut off from that push, so it's safer to change a bulb.

In many homes you can turn on a staircase light at the bottom and switch it off at the top. That trick uses two-way switches. Each one can send the current down either of two wires. The light is on when both switches point to the same wire and off when they don't. Flip either one and you change the answer.

This is a simple bit of logic, the same yes-or-no kind computers use with [[@binary-code|binary]]. Hotels and long corridors use a third type, called an intermediate switch, so three or more places can control one light.

When the current arrives, an old-style [[@light-bulb|bulb]] heats a thin wire until it glows white-hot. An LED bulb has a small circuit in its base that turns the mains supply into a gentle, steady flow for its light-emitting chips. That's why some LEDs take a fraction of a second to come on.

Every circuit in a house also passes through a [[@fuses-switches|fuse or circuit breaker]]. If too much current flows, it cuts the power before the wires get dangerously hot. Your light switch is the small gate. The breaker is the guard at the main door.

text: A zip has two strips of cloth tape, each with a row of small teeth along one edge. Every tooth has a little bump on its top and a hollow on its bottom. When the bump of one tooth fits into the hollow of the tooth above it on the other side, the two rows lock together like fingers clasped tight.

The teeth can't do this on their own. They need to meet at exactly the right angle. That is the job of the slider, the small metal piece you pull. Inside it is a Y-shaped channel. As you pull it up, the two arms of the Y guide the teeth in from each side and press them together one at a time. Pull it down, and a small wedge in the middle pushes the teeth apart again.

st.prompt: Without the slider, can you join the two sides of a zip by pressing the teeth together with your fingers?

options.t: Hardly. The teeth have to meet at an angle, which the slider does for you
Yes, but only with a metal zip

st.reveal: Each tooth has a bump on top and a hollow underneath. They only hook together if they come in at a slant, one after another, which is exactly what the Y-shaped channel inside the slider does. Pressed together flat, they mostly bump and slip.

d.try: Look closely at a zip on a bag or jacket, using a magnifying glass if you have one. Find the bump on top of each tooth and the hollow underneath. Open the zip halfway, then slowly close it while watching how the teeth swing in from each side and hook one by one inside the slider.
myth: The zip was invented for trousers.
Early zips were used on boots, gloves, money belts and tobacco pouches. Tailors were slow to trust them in clothes. Zips in trousers became common only in the 1930s.
facts: from a 1923 rubber boot made by B.F. Goodrich
YKK of Japan, whose letters appear on many zips

sec.t:
In 1893, the American inventor Whitcomb Judson patented a "clasp locker". He is often said to have shown it at the World's Fair in Chicago that year. It used hooks and eyes that a slider joined together, and it was meant to save people the trouble of buttoning their high boots.

It was clever, but it didn't work well. The hooks popped open at awkward moments, and they rusted. Very few people bought one. A clothing fastener that might fly open in the street was not something many people wanted to risk. Judson's company kept trying, and in 1906 it hired a young Swedish-born engineer named Gideon Sundback.

Through the 1920s, zips appeared on boots, purses and tobacco pouches. Tailors still preferred buttons for clothes. In the 1930s, [[@fashion-history|fashion]] designers and makers of children's clothing began promoting zips as easier to use, and men's trousers started using them.

Today zips are everywhere, from [[@jeans|jeans]] to [[@life-school-bags|school bags]], tents and sleeping bags. Some are made of metal, some of plastic and some are a tight coil of nylon. A Japanese company, YKK, makes a very large share of them. Check the slider of a zip near you and there's a fair chance you'll see those three letters.

If one tooth is bent or missing, the teeth below it can't hook properly and the zip splits open behind the slider. Sometimes the slider has simply worn loose, and the Y-channel no longer squeezes hard enough. A tailor can often fix it by gently pinching the slider tighter or fitting a new one.

Engineers still work on zips. Divers' drysuits and [[@spacesuits|spacesuits]] have needed special airtight zips, with rubber seals so no water or air can get through. The basic idea is the same Sundback worked out more than a century ago: get each tooth in at the right angle, and let [[@friction|friction]] and shape hold it there.

किसी पुराने शहर को चुनने के बजाय भारत के नेताओं ने बिल्कुल नया शहर बनाने का फ़ैसला किया। प्रधानमंत्री [[@nehru|नेहरू]] चाहते थे कि यह शहर अतीत से बँधा न रहे, बल्कि एक आज़ाद, आधुनिक भारत की पहचान बने। शहर का नाम पास के चंडी मंदिर पर पड़ा, जो देवी चंडी का मंदिर है। इसका मुख्य नक्शा 1950 के दशक की शुरुआत में [[architecture|वास्तुकार]] ल कॉर्बूज़िए ने बनाया।

sec.t:
ल कॉर्बूज़िए ने चंडीगढ़ को सड़कों की एक ऐसी व्यवस्था दी जिसे वे "7 वी" कहते थे। तेज़ सड़कें सेक्टरों के बीच से गुज़रती थीं, धीमी गलियाँ उनके अंदर घूमती थीं, और पैदल रास्तों और साइकिल पटरियों के अपने अलग रास्ते थे। मकसद था कि [[@road-safety|तेज़ ट्रैफ़िक उन जगहों से दूर रहे]] जहाँ बच्चे पैदल स्कूल जाते हैं।

शहर के बीच से लंबी हरी पट्टियाँ गुज़रती हैं, और सड़कों के किनारे हज़ारों पेड़ लगाए गए। सुखना झील, जो एक बरसाती नाले पर बाँध बनाकर तैयार किया गया [[reservoir|जलाशय]] है, लोगों को टहलने और नाव चलाने की जगह देती है।

आलोचक बताते हैं कि यह योजना पूरी तरह सही नहीं थी। शहर लगभग 5 लाख लोगों के लिए बनाया गया था, पर इसकी आबादी इससे कहीं आगे निकल चुकी है, और मोहाली और पंचकूला जैसे आसपास के शहर इसके चारों ओर फैल गए हैं। कुछ लोगों को लंबी, चौड़ी सड़कें पैदल पार करना भी मुश्किल लगता है। योजनाकार आज भी यहाँ आकर पढ़ते हैं कि क्या चला और क्या नहीं।

{{story:recycling}}

शहर के सिरे पर, शिवालिक की पहाड़ियों के सामने, ल कॉर्बूज़िए ने कैपिटल कॉम्प्लेक्स डिज़ाइन किया। इसमें हाई कोर्ट, विधानसभा और सचिवालय हैं, जो खुरदरे, दमदार कंक्रीट से बने हैं। पास ही ओपन हैंड मॉन्यूमेंट खड़ा है, धातु का एक विशाल हाथ जो हवा के साथ घूमता है। 2016 में यह कॉम्प्लेक्स उस यूनेस्को विश्व धरोहर स्थल का हिस्सा बना जिसमें सात देशों में फैला ल कॉर्बूज़िए का काम शामिल है।

बाद में चंडीगढ़ को एक दूसरी भूमिका भी मिली। 1966 में जब हरियाणा बना, तो यह शहर पंजाब और हरियाणा दोनों की राजधानी बन गया, और साथ ही केंद्र सरकार के अधीन चलने वाला एक केंद्र शासित प्रदेश भी।

जब शहर बन रहा था, तब नेक चंद नाम के एक सड़क निरीक्षक ने कबाड़ जमा करना शुरू किया: टूटी टाइलें, बोतलें, बिजली के पुर्ज़े, चूड़ियाँ और शौचालय की सीटें। जंगल के एक कोने में उन्होंने चुपचाप इनसे इंसानों और जानवरों की सैकड़ों [[sculpture|मूर्तियाँ]] बना डालीं।

1975 में जब अफ़सरों को यह बगीचा मिला, तो कानूनी तौर पर यह ग़ैर-कानूनी था। पर लोगों को यह बहुत पसंद आया, और शहर ने इसे बचाने का फ़ैसला किया। आज रॉक गार्डन चंडीगढ़ की सबसे ज़्यादा देखी जाने वाली जगहों में से एक है, एक ऐसी कलाकृति जो लगभग पूरी की पूरी उन चीज़ों से बनी है जिन्हें योजना से बसे इस शहर ने फेंक दिया था। [[@urban-planning|शहरी योजनाकार]] आज भी इसकी मिसाल देते हैं: सबसे सावधानी से खींचा गया शहर भी ऐसे ढंग से बढ़ता है जिसकी किसी ने योजना नहीं बनाई थी।

text: The violin came to South India with Europeans in the 1700s. In Madras, now Chennai, and in royal courts like Thanjavur, Indian musicians heard it in military bands and at European gatherings. In the early 1800s, a few gifted musicians began playing Carnatic music on it.

They found that the violin could do something many Indian instruments found hard: hold a long note and slide smoothly between notes, just like a singer's voice. So they changed how it was held and tuned, and made it their own. Today the violin is the standard instrument accompanying singers in [[@carnatic-hindustani|Carnatic concerts]].

st.prompt: Why do Carnatic violinists hold the violin resting on their foot instead of under the chin?

options.t: It frees the left hand to slide and shake notes smoothly
Carnatic violins are too heavy to lift
It makes the violin much louder

st.reveal: Carnatic music is full of gamakas, notes that slide, bend and wobble. With the violin braced between chest and foot, the left hand can slide freely up and down the neck. Sitting on the floor also matches how other Carnatic musicians perform.

n.certNote: Historians agree the violin entered Carnatic music in the early 1800s. Who did it first is debated, with Baluswami Dikshitar and Vadivelu of the Thanjavur Quartet both given credit by different sources.

d.try: Stretch a rubber band around an open box or a plastic container. Pluck it, then press the band down with one finger at different points and pluck again. Now slide your finger along while it is still ringing. That sliding sound is a little like a gamaka on the Carnatic violin.
myth: The violin in Carnatic music is played exactly the way Western violinists play it.
It is the same instrument, but Carnatic players sit on the floor, rest it on the foot, tune it differently and use sliding notes that Western classical music rarely uses.
facts: two strings to Sa and two to Pa
accompanying the singer, also played solo

sec.t:
Two names are linked with the violin's arrival. One is Baluswami Dikshitar, younger brother of the great composer Muthuswami Dikshitar. He is said to have learned the violin from a European musician in Madras and then adapted it for Carnatic music.

The other is Vadivelu, one of four brothers from Thanjavur known as the Thanjavur Quartet, who served at the court of Maharaja Swathi Thirunal of Travancore. He was a brilliant violinist, and the Maharaja is said to have given him an ivory violin. Different sources give different credit, and both men probably played a part.

Muthuswami Dikshitar himself enjoyed the Western band music he heard in Madras. He wrote a set of short Sanskrit songs, called *nottuswaram*, set to Western band tunes.

In a concert, the violinist sits to the singer's side, often with a mridangam drummer on the other. The violinist follows the singer almost note for note, repeating phrases a moment later and filling in when the singer pauses for breath. During improvised parts, the singer and violinist take turns, answering each other like a conversation.

It takes great skill, because the violinist often doesn't know exactly what the singer will do next. Good accompanists learn hundreds of compositions and [[raga|ragas]] so that they can follow anywhere.

In the 1900s, violinists became stars in their own right. Mysore T. Chowdiah used a violin with seven strings for a deeper, fuller sound. Lalgudi G. Jayaraman composed many pieces and was known for making the violin sound almost like singing. T. N. Krishnan and M. S. Gopalakrishnan were famous soloists, and A. Kanyakumari has accompanied leading singers for decades.

L. Subramaniam mixed Carnatic music with jazz and [[@classical-western|Western classical music]], playing with orchestras around the world. The violin is now used in Hindustani music too: N. Rajam developed a style that imitates the human voice.

Today, December in [[@chennai|Chennai]] is concert season, when hundreds of performances fill the city's music halls. On almost every stage, the violin sits beside the singer and the drums. An instrument that once played European marches now helps carry ragas composed centuries ago. The [[@veena|veena]] and the human voice are far older in Carnatic music, but the violin has earned its seat beside them. Many young students in Chennai, Bengaluru and among Indian families in the USA now pick it as their first instrument.

text: [[climate|Climate]] change is mostly caused by burning coal, oil and gas for electricity, transport and factories. That releases [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]] and other gases that trap heat around the Earth. Fixing it needs big changes, like clean power stations and better buses and trains, and those are decided by governments and companies.

Kids can still help, in three main ways. They can waste less energy and food at home. They can learn how the problem works and explain it to others. And they can speak up, at school, in their neighbourhood and, one day, at the voting booth. The last one may matter most.

st.prompt: Which of these causes the most heat-trapping gas in a typical day for a city family?

options.t: Electricity and fuel for transport and cooking

st.reveal: Energy for travel, cooling, cooking and running the home usually adds up to far more than small plastic items or chargers. Plastic matters for oceans and wildlife, but its share of climate warming is smaller.

src: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), Sixth Assessment Report, Summary for Policymakers (2023).
UN Environment Programme, Food Waste Index Report 2024.
n.certNote: Scientists agree that climate change is real and caused mainly by people. They and others disagree about which actions matter most, and about how much individual choices count compared with big changes by governments and companies.

d.try: Do a one-week energy hunt at home. Make a chart of every device that runs on electricity or fuel, mark which ones are used most, and pick two easy changes, such as turning off fans in empty rooms or walking to a nearby shop. Share the chart with your family.
myth: One person's actions are too small to matter at all.

One person can't fix climate change alone, but people's choices add up and spread. Habits rub off on friends and family, and when many people ask for change, schools, companies and governments listen.

sec.h: Start with what you can see
sec.t:
Some of the biggest everyday sources of [[greenhouse-gas|greenhouse gases]] are hidden inside ordinary things. An air conditioner set to 18 °C uses much more power than one set to 24 °C. In India, most electricity still comes from coal, so every unit saved means less coal burned.

Food matters too. About a fifth of the food that reaches shops, restaurants and homes worldwide is wasted, according to the UN's 2024 report. Much of it rots in dumps and gives off methane, which is why [[@food-waste|food waste]] is a climate problem as well as a hunger one. Taking only what you'll eat, and finishing leftovers, is a small habit with a real effect. Travel adds up as well. Walking, cycling, taking the school bus or sharing a ride all cut fuel use.

sec.h: Small things that matter less than you'd think

sec.t:
Many of the decisions that shape climate change are made in meetings far away, but those meetings respond to people. In 2018, a Swedish schoolgirl began sitting outside her country's [[parliament|parliament]] on Fridays. Within a year, millions of students in many countries had joined school strikes for climate, a story told in [[@greta-and-youth|young people changing the world]].

You don't need a protest sign to speak up. Students have asked their schools to plant trees, set up composting or put solar panels on the roof. Some have written letters to local leaders about safe cycle lanes. Long before any of this, villagers in the Himalayas protected their forests in the [[@chipko|Chipko movement]], showing that ordinary people can change official plans.

sec.h: Learning to tell good information from bad
sec.t:
Climate change attracts a lot of false claims online, both ones saying it isn't happening and ones saying it's already too late. Neither is true. Scientists, through groups like the IPCC, agree that warming is real, caused mainly by people, and that every bit of warming avoided reduces harm.

Learning to check sources is a climate skill. Ask who made a claim, what their evidence is, and whether scientists agree.

There are real signs of progress. [[@renewable-energy|Solar power]] has become much cheaper since 2010, and India has built huge solar parks in Rajasthan and Gujarat. India and many other countries have set targets for net zero, when a country's emissions are balanced by what is removed from the air. India aims for 2070. Countries' plans can change, and they need people watching to make sure they are kept. Today's 10-year-olds will be about 54 in 2070, and they will be the adults in charge of reaching that goal.

text: Maurits Cornelis Escher, born in the Netherlands in 1898, made prints that look like puzzles. Lizards crawl out of a flat pattern and back in. Monks walk up a staircase that never ends. Birds slowly turn into fish. Water flows downhill and arrives back where it started.

Behind each picture is a maths idea. He used [[@tessellations|tessellations]], shapes that fit together with no gaps. He used [[@symmetry|symmetry]], turning and flipping shapes. He played with [[@infinity|infinity]] and drew impossible objects. Escher never studied maths and said he couldn't follow the formulas, yet he explored these ideas by drawing them.

st.prompt: In Escher's print Waterfall, water flows down a channel, turns a wheel, and then ends up back at the top. How is this possible?

options.t: It isn't possible; the drawing tricks your eye with an impossible shape
A hidden pump pushes the water up

st.reveal: Each small part of Waterfall looks correct, but the whole thing is built on an impossible triangle, a shape first described by the mathematicians Lionel and Roger Penrose. Your brain checks the drawing piece by piece and misses the trick.

d.try: Cut a square of card. Cut a curvy shape out of one side and tape it onto the opposite side. Trace the new shape on paper again and again so the pieces fit together with no gaps. Add eyes and legs, and you have your own Escher-style tessellation.
myth: Escher was a trained mathematician who used formulas to plan his art.

Escher had no maths training and did poorly in school maths. He worked out his patterns by drawing and experimenting, and later swapped ideas with real mathematicians like H. S. M. Coxeter and Roger Penrose.

sec.t:
As a student, Escher wasn't a star. He failed some of his school exams and dropped out of [[architecture|architecture]] school to study graphic art instead.

In 1922, and again in 1936, he visited the [[@alhambra|Alhambra]] in Granada, Spain. Its walls are covered with Islamic tile patterns that repeat endlessly in clever ways. Escher spent days copying them. The tile makers used only abstract shapes, because many Islamic artists avoided drawing living things. Escher wondered: what if the shapes were animals?

He spent years learning how. Mathematicians later showed that there are exactly 17 basic ways to repeat a pattern across a flat surface. Escher found his way to many of them without knowing the theory, by trial and error and lots of sketching. He filled notebooks with his own rules, colour-coded and numbered, like a scientist's lab book.

Escher wanted to show infinity inside a frame. In 1958, the Canadian mathematician H. S. M. Coxeter sent him a paper with a diagram of triangles that got smaller and smaller towards the edge of a circle. Escher couldn't follow the text, but the picture struck him at once. He later wrote that it gave him quite a shock.

He used it to create his Circle Limit prints, where fish or angels and devils shrink towards the edge without ever reaching it. Mathematicians call this hyperbolic [[geometry|geometry]]. Coxeter later checked one print and found that Escher's drawing was more accurate than the artist could have known.

In Möbius Strip II (1963), nine red ants crawl around a twisted loop. Follow one and you'll see it covers both "sides" without crossing an edge, because a [[@puzzle-mobius|Möbius strip]] has only one side.

Escher made about 450 prints and more than 2,000 drawings before he died in 1972. Today his art appears on maths textbooks, album covers and film sets. The film *Inception* even featured a Penrose staircase. And the same tile-fitting tricks that Escher loved can be found under your feet, in floors made of hexagons, the shape bees also choose for their [[@honeycomb|honeycombs]].

text: Chess pieces move the way they do because the game is a frozen army from ancient India. About 1,500 years ago, people played *chaturanga*, a battle game with four parts of an army: foot soldiers, horses, elephants and chariots. Each piece moved a bit like the real thing.

As the game travelled to Persia, then the Arab world, then Europe, players kept changing the rules. Some pieces got new names. A few got new powers. The moves you learn today are the result of that long relay, settled in Europe only about 500 years ago.

st.prompt: Which chess piece used to be one of the weakest on the board?
st.reveal: In older versions of chess, the queen was a royal adviser who could move only one square diagonally. Around the late 1400s, players in Spain and Italy let her sweep across the board, and she became the strongest piece.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Chess.

n.certNote: Most historians agree chess grew out of the Indian game chaturanga, but early rules were not written down clearly, so some old moves, like the elephant's, are educated guesses.

d.try: Play a game with a friend using the old rules. Your queen may move only one square diagonally, and your bishops jump exactly two squares diagonally. Notice how much slower and more careful the game becomes.
myth: The queen has always been the most powerful piece in chess.
For most of chess history she was one of the weakest. Her long-range moves only arrived in Europe around 500 years ago.

sec.h: The elephant that became a bishop
sec.t:
The strangest change happened to the elephant. In chaturanga it probably jumped exactly two squares diagonally. Arab players called it *al-fil*, the elephant. Spanish players still call the bishop *alfil* today.

In Europe, few people had seen an elephant. The piece's two little bumps, which were meant to be tusks, looked like a bishop's pointed hat. In England the elephant became a churchman. In France it became a jester. Its jump turned into a long diagonal glide around the same time the queen changed.

Other pieces got new identities too. The Persian name for the king, *shah*, gave us the word "check". The cry *shah mat*, often translated as "the king is helpless", became "checkmate". So every time a player says it, they are speaking a little Persian. In Russian the bishop is still called *slon*, the elephant, so the old animal never fully left the board.

The queen started as a male minister, the *mantri* in India and the *ferz* in Persia. He stood beside the king and stepped one square diagonally. He was so weak that a single knight was worth far more.

Then, in the late 1400s, players in Spain and Italy tried something new. They let the queen move any distance in any straight line. Games that once took hours of slow shuffling became sharp and fast. Some called the new game "the queen's chess" or even "mad queen chess". Within about 50 years it had swept across Europe, and the old rules faded away.

A few rules are newer still. Pawns gained the right to step two squares on their first move, to speed up the slow opening. Castling, where the king tucks behind a rook in one move, became standard a few centuries ago. Even the shape of the pieces was fixed late. The design used in almost every [[tournament|tournament]], the Staunton set, appeared in London in 1849.

Chess also came home. India now produces some of the strongest players on Earth, and the story of [[@viswanathan-anand|Viswanathan Anand]] and the young [[grandmaster|grandmasters]] who followed him is a good one. Chaturanga's [[@elephants-india|elephants]] may have lost their tusks, but every game still starts with an ancient Indian army. And the board hides one more secret. Put one grain of rice on the first square and double it on each square after. By the last square you need more rice than the whole world grows in centuries, which is the trick behind the famous [[@puzzle-chessboard-rice|chessboard rice puzzle]].

text: इसका श्रेय आम तौर पर इग्नाज़ ज़ेमेलवाइस को दिया जाता है, जो हंगरी के डॉक्टर थे और ऑस्ट्रिया के वियना में काम करते थे। 1847 में उन्होंने अपने प्रसूति वार्ड के डॉक्टरों और छात्रों से कहा कि माँओं की जाँच से पहले वे क्लोरीन के घोल में हाथ धोएँ। प्रसूति ज्वर नाम के एक जानलेवा [[infection|संक्रमण]] से होने वाली मौतें हर 10 में से लगभग 1 माँ से घटकर हर 100 में से 1 या 2 के आसपास आ गईं।

उस समय किसी को नहीं पता था कि बीमारियाँ कीटाणुओं से होती हैं। ज़ेमेलवाइस ने अंदाज़ा लगाया कि कोई अनदेखी चीज़ डॉक्टरों के हाथों पर सवार होकर जा रही है। बहुत-से बड़े डॉक्टरों ने उनकी बात मानने से इनकार कर दिया। अस्पतालों में हाथ धोना आम होने में दशकों लगे, और लुई पाश्चर व जोसेफ़ लिस्टर जैसे वैज्ञानिकों का काम भी।

st.prompt: ज़ेमेलवाइस के अस्पताल में एक वार्ड डॉक्टर चलाते थे और एक दाइयाँ। 1847 से पहले किस वार्ड में ज़्यादा माँओं की मौत होती थी?
st.reveal: डॉक्टरों वाला वार्ड कहीं ज़्यादा जानलेवा था। डॉक्टर और छात्र अक्सर लाशों की जाँच करके सीधे वहाँ आ जाते थे, और उनके हाथों पर अनदेखे कीटाणु होते थे। दाइयाँ यह काम नहीं करती थीं।

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ignaz Semmelweis.

sec.t:
वियना जनरल अस्पताल में प्रसूति के दो क्लिनिक थे। एक डॉक्टर और मेडिकल छात्र चलाते थे, दूसरा दाइयाँ। माँएँ जानती थीं कि कौन-सा कौन है। कुछ गिड़गिड़ाती थीं कि उन्हें दाइयों वाले वार्ड में भेजा जाए, और कुछ तो डॉक्टरों वाले वार्ड में जाने की बजाय सड़क पर ही बच्चे को जन्म दे देती थीं।

उनका डरना ठीक था। डॉक्टरों वाले क्लिनिक में कुछ सालों में हर 10 में से लगभग 1 माँ प्रसूति ज्वर से मर जाती थी। दाइयों वाले क्लिनिक में यह गिनती कहीं कम थी। ज़ेमेलवाइस चकरा गए। वही शहर, वही अस्पताल, वैसे ही मरीज़।

मई 1847 में उन्होंने वार्ड के दरवाज़े पर क्लोरीन मिले चूने के घोल का एक कटोरा रखवा दिया। हर किसी को तब तक हाथ रगड़ने पड़ते थे जब तक लाशघर की गंध न चली जाए। कुछ ही महीनों में उनके क्लिनिक में मौतें तेज़ी से गिरकर हर 100 में से 1 या 2 के आसपास आ गईं।

वे हर साल सैकड़ों जानें बचा रहे थे, पर समझा नहीं पा रहे थे कि यह काम क्यों करता है। बहुत-से डॉक्टरों को यह बात अपमान लगी कि मौत खुद वही फैला रहे हैं। ज़ेमेलवाइस ने अपने आलोचकों पर गुस्से भरी चिट्ठियाँ भी लिखीं, जिससे उनके दोस्त कम ही बने। उनकी वियना वाली नौकरी चली गई और वे बुडापेस्ट लौट गए। 1865 में 47 साल की उम्र में उनकी मौत हो गई, और तब तक उनके विचारों को ज़्यादातर अनदेखा ही किया जा रहा था।

वे अकेले नहीं थे। अमेरिका के बोस्टन में डॉक्टर और लेखक ओलिवर वेंडेल होम्स ने 1843 में ही कहा था कि प्रसूति ज्वर डॉक्टरों से फैलता है। उन पर भी बड़े प्रोफ़ेसरों ने हमला बोला।

सबूत 1860 के दशक में आया। लुई पाश्चर ने दिखाया कि [[@microscopes|सूक्ष्मदर्शी]] से दिखने वाले नन्हे जीव चीज़ों के सड़ने और बीमारियों की वजह हैं। ब्रिटेन में जोसेफ़ लिस्टर ने घावों और औज़ारों को साफ़ करने के लिए कार्बोलिक एसिड का इस्तेमाल किया, और ऑपरेशन से होने वाली मौतें घट गईं। कीटाणुओं को समझने वाली [[@history-of-medicine|चिकित्सा]] का दौर शुरू हो गया था।

sec.h: साबुन आज भी क्यों ज़रूरी है
sec.t:
आज हम जानते हैं कि हम जो भी छूते हैं, उससे हाथों पर [[bacteria|बैक्टीरिया]] और [[virus|वायरस]] आ जाते हैं। साबुन के [[molecule|अणुओं]] का एक सिरा चिकनाई को पकड़ता है और दूसरा पानी से प्यार करता है। ये कीटाणुओं को त्वचा से खींचकर लपेट लेते हैं, ताकि पानी उन्हें बहा ले जाए। [[@soap-germs|साबुन और कीटाणु]] में इसे और विस्तार से समझाया गया है।

सेहत के जानकार कहते हैं कि साबुन से हाथ धोने पर पेट के संक्रमण लगभग एक-तिहाई तक घट सकते हैं। 2020 की कोविड-19 [[pandemic|महामारी]] के दौरान चेन्नई से शिकागो तक के बच्चों ने 20 सेकंड तक हाथ रगड़ना सीखा, अक्सर कोई छोटा-सा गाना दो बार गुनगुनाते हुए।

विश्व स्वास्थ्य संगठन और यूनिसेफ़ अब हर 15 अक्टूबर को विश्व हाथ धुलाई दिवस मनाने को बढ़ावा देते हैं। अस्पतालों में हर बिस्तर के पास हैंड जेल रखा होता है। ज़ेमेलवाइस का क्लोरीन वाला कटोरा इतिहास में जान बचाने के सबसे सस्ते तरीकों में से एक निकला। और तुम्हारी अपनी त्वचा पर इतने [[@gross-body-bacteria|बैक्टीरिया]] रहते हैं जितने शायद तुम जानना भी न चाहो।

text: सेहतमंद बड़े लोग शायद ही कभी लगभग 2.1 मीटर से ज़्यादा लंबे होते हैं। इससे ज़्यादा लंबे लोगों में लगभग हमेशा ऐसी हालत होती है जिसमें शरीर ज़रूरत से ज़्यादा ग्रोथ [[hormone|हॉर्मोन]] बनाता है। आम तौर पर इसकी वजह पिट्यूटरी पर एक छोटी, बेनुकसान गाँठ होती है। पिट्यूटरी दिमाग के निचले सिरे पर मटर के दाने जितनी एक [[gland|ग्रंथि]] है।

अब तक भरोसेमंद ढंग से नापे गए सबसे लंबे इंसान थे रॉबर्ट वैडलो, जो अमेरिका के इलिनॉय राज्य के ऑल्टन शहर के थे। 1940 में उनकी लंबाई 2.72 मीटर थी, यानी एक आम दरवाज़े से भी ऊँचे, और ऊपर से आधा मीटर और। वैज्ञानिकों को लगता है कि इंसानी शरीर सुरक्षित रूप से इससे बहुत आगे नहीं जा सकता। इतने बड़े आकार और वज़न को सँभालने में दिल, हड्डियों और जोड़ों को बहुत मुश्किल होती है।

sec.h: वह लड़का जो बढ़ता ही गया

sec.t:
बड़े आकार से परेशानियाँ एक सीधे-से गणित की वजह से आती हैं। अगर किसी इंसान की लंबाई दुगनी कर दो, तो उसका शरीर लगभग आठ गुना भारी हो जाता है, पर उसकी हड्डियाँ बस लगभग चार गुना मज़बूत होती हैं। हड्डी की ताकत उसकी लंबाई से नहीं, उसकी मोटाई, यानी कटे हुए सिरे के क्षेत्रफल से तय होती है।

दिल का काम भी बढ़ जाता है। उसे [[gravity|गुरुत्वाकर्षण]] के खिलाफ़ खून को और ऊपर दिमाग तक पंप करना पड़ता है। [[@power-giraffe-neck|जिराफ़]] यह मुश्किल एक बड़े, मोटी दीवारों वाले दिल और बहुत ऊँचे ब्लड प्रेशर से सुलझाता है। इंसान इस तरह नहीं बने हैं। बहुत लंबे लोगों को अक्सर दिल की तकलीफ़, जोड़ों का दर्द और चलने में दिक्कत होती है।

बच्चे अपनी लंबी हड्डियों के सिरों पर बढ़ते हैं, उन नरम हिस्सों में जिन्हें ग्रोथ प्लेट कहते हैं। ये [[cartilage|उपास्थि]], यानी नरम हड्डी, से बनी होती हैं, जो धीरे-धीरे पक्की हड्डी में बदलती जाती है। ग्रोथ हॉर्मोन और दूसरे संकेत बचपन भर, और किशोर उम्र के बड़े उछाल में भी, इन प्लेटों को काम में लगाए रखते हैं।

किशोरावस्था के आखिरी सालों तक ग्रोथ प्लेटें बंद होकर ठोस हड्डी बन जाती हैं। इसके बाद तुम कितना भी खाओ या खिंचाव करो, और लंबे नहीं हो सकते। डॉक्टर एक्स-रे में देख सकते हैं कि बच्चे की [[@bones-growth|हड्डियाँ अभी बढ़ रही हैं]] या नहीं।

पिछली एक सदी में दुनिया भर के लोग लंबे हुए हैं, ज़्यादातर बेहतर खाने और बचपन की कम बीमारियों की वजह से। नीदरलैंड्स के पुरुषों की औसत लंबाई अब लगभग 1.83 मीटर है, जो दुनिया में सबसे ज़्यादा है। 1850 के दशक के बाद से यह लगभग 20 सेमी बढ़ी है। दक्षिण कोरिया की महिलाएँ एक सदी में लगभग 20 सेमी लंबी हुईं, जो अब तक नापी गई सबसे बड़ी छलाँगों में से एक है।

भारत के बड़े भी लंबे हुए हैं, हालाँकि धीरे-धीरे, और हाल के कुछ दशकों में औसत लंबाई मुश्किल से बदली। वैज्ञानिक लंबाई को इस बात का आईना मानते हैं कि कोई देश अपने बच्चों को कितना अच्छा खिलाता है। अगर किसी पूरी आबादी की लंबाई कम हो, तो इसकी वजह आम तौर पर बचपन का कमज़ोर खाना या बीमारी होती है, जीन नहीं।

2026 तक दुनिया के सबसे लंबे जीवित पुरुष तुर्किये के सुल्तान कोसेन हैं, जिनकी लंबाई 2.51 मीटर है। 2010 में एक ऑपरेशन से उनका बढ़ना रोका गया। अमेरिका की बास्केटबॉल लीग, [[@basketball|एनबीए]], में 2.2 मीटर से लंबे खिलाड़ी कम ही होते हैं, और इतिहास के सबसे लंबे खिलाड़ी लगभग 2.31 मीटर के रहे हैं।

जुड़वाँ बच्चों पर हुए अध्ययन बताते हैं कि लोगों की लंबाई में जो फ़र्क होता है, उसका लगभग 80% उनके [[@genes-family|जीन]] से आता है। इसीलिए लंबे माता-पिता के बच्चे अक्सर लंबे होते हैं। पर सबसे लंबे माता-पिता और सबसे अच्छे खाने के बावजूद, इंसानी शरीर अपनी हदों से बहुत पहले टकरा जाता है, जिराफ़ की ऊँचाई से तो बहुत पहले, जो लगभग 5 मीटर ऊँचा होता है।

sec.t:
नींद लगभग 90 मिनट के चक्रों में आती है। पहले तुम हल्की नींद में जाते हो, फिर [[@body-sleepwalking|गहरी नींद]] में। तब साँस धीमी हो जाती है और तुम्हें जगाना मुश्किल होता है। बढ़त वाला ज़्यादातर हॉर्मोन शरीर इसी गहरी नींद में छोड़ता है।

फिर आती है REM नींद। REM का मतलब है "रैपिड आई मूवमेंट", यानी आँखों की तेज़ हलचल। बंद पलकों के नीचे आँखें इधर-उधर फड़कती हैं, दिमाग़ बहुत सक्रिय हो जाता है, और ज़्यादातर साफ़-साफ़ [[@dreams|सपने]] इसी समय आते हैं। एक आम रात में ऐसे चार से छह चक्र होते हैं। शुरू में गहरी नींद ज़्यादा होती है और सुबह की तरफ़ REM नींद।

सोते समय दिमाग़ सीखी हुई चीज़ों को दोहराता और पक्का करता लगता है। प्रयोगों में, जो लोग शब्दों की सूची या कोई नया हुनर सीखने के बाद सोते हैं, वे आमतौर पर जागते रहने वालों से बेहतर याद रखते हैं। नींद ताज़ा अनुभवों को टिकाऊ [[@memory|यादों]] में बदलने में मदद करती है।

चूहों पर हुए अध्ययन बताते हैं कि नींद शायद दिमाग़ से बेकार रसायनों को बाहर निकालने में भी मदद करती है, जैसे रात की पाली में काम करने वाले सफ़ाई कर्मचारी। वैज्ञानिक अभी जाँच रहे हैं कि इंसानों में ऐसा कितना होता है।

नींद शरीर को कीटाणुओं से लड़ने में भी मदद करती है। अमेरिका के एक प्रयोग में स्वयंसेवकों को जानबूझकर ज़ुकाम का [[virus|वायरस]] दिया गया। जो लोग आमतौर पर रात में छह घंटे से कम सोते थे, उन्हें सात घंटे या ज़्यादा सोने वालों के मुकाबले ज़ुकाम पकड़ने की आशंका ज़्यादा थी।

चक्रों के बीच थोड़ी देर के लिए जाग जाना सामान्य है। ज़्यादातर लोग रात में कुछ बार ऐसा करते हैं और उन्हें कभी याद भी नहीं रहता।

{{story:day-night}}

दिमाग़ के अंदर गहराई में कोशिकाओं का एक नन्हा-सा गुच्छा है, जो लगभग 24 घंटे वाली [[@clocks|घड़ी]] का काम करता है। आँखों तक पहुँचने वाली रोशनी इसे [[@day-night|दिन और रात]] के साथ ताल में रखती है। अँधेरा होने पर शरीर ज़्यादा मेलाटोनिन बनाता है। यह वह रसायन है जिससे नींद आने लगती है।

देर रात की चमकती स्क्रीन इस घड़ी को उलझा सकती है और नींद को आगे खिसका सकती है। दुनिया के उस पार हवाई सफ़र भी इसे उलझा देता है। दिल्ली से न्यूयॉर्क उड़ो, तो कई दिनों तक तुम्हारा शरीर भारत के समय पर ही चलता रहता है। वही भारी-भारी, ऊँघता-सा एहसास [[@jet-lag|जेट लैग]] है।

1964 में अमेरिका के सैन डिएगो में 17 साल का रैंडी गार्डनर स्कूल के एक विज्ञान प्रोजेक्ट के लिए लगभग 11 दिन तक जागता रहा। दिन बीतते गए और वह चिड़चिड़ा होता गया, उसे ध्यान लगाने में दिक्कत होने लगी और चीज़ें याद रखना मुश्किल हो गया। प्रयोग ख़त्म होने के बाद वह लगभग 14 घंटे सोया और ठीक हो गया। बाद में रिकॉर्ड की किताबों ने ऐसी कोशिशें दर्ज करना बंद कर दिया, क्योंकि बिना सोए रहना ख़तरनाक है।

नींद के जानकार 6 से 12 साल के बच्चों के लिए रात में 9 से 12 घंटे, और किशोरों के लिए 8 से 10 घंटे की नींद सुझाते हैं। बड़ों को लगभग 7 घंटे या उससे ज़्यादा चाहिए। छोटे शिशु तो दिन का ज़्यादातर हिस्सा सोते ही रहते हैं।

जानवरों में बहुत फ़र्क है। कुछ [[@bats-fly|चमगादड़]] दिन में लगभग 20 घंटे सोते हैं, जबकि जिराफ़ शायद बस कुछ ही घंटे सो पाते हैं। [[@dolphins-click|डॉल्फ़िन]] तो कभी पूरी तरह ढीली पड़ती ही नहीं। इंसानों के लिए अच्छी नींद के सबसे आसान नुस्ख़े हैं: रोज़ एक तय समय पर सोना, अँधेरा कमरा, और सोने से ठीक पहले स्क्रीन से दूरी।

text: A yawn is a slow, deep breath in with your mouth wide open, a stretch of the jaw and face, then a shorter breath out. Everyone yawns, and so do most animals with a backbone. We yawn more when we're sleepy, bored or just waking up.

The strange part is that yawns spread. When you see someone yawn, there's a good chance you'll yawn too, often within a few seconds. Scientists call this contagious yawning. They aren't sure why it happens. The most popular ideas are that it's linked to how we tune in to other people, or that it helps a group of animals become alert or sleepy together.

st.prompt: In a famous experiment, people breathed air with extra oxygen in it. What happened to how often they yawned?
st.reveal: In the 1980s, psychologist Robert Provine tested the old idea that we yawn to get more oxygen. Extra oxygen made no difference to yawning, and neither did extra carbon dioxide. So yawns probably do some other job.

src.Provine R. R. (2012) Curious Behavior: Yawning, Laughing, Hiccupping, and Beyond. Harvard University Press.

src: Joly-Mascheroni R. M. et al. (2008) Dogs catch human yawns. Biology Letters.
Gallup A. C. and Gallup G. G. (2007) Yawning as a brain cooling mechanism. Evolutionary Psychology.
n.certNote: Scientists agree that yawns spread from person to person, but not on why. Ideas about empathy, brain cooling and keeping groups alert each have some evidence, and none is settled.

sec.t:
For a long time, people thought we yawn because our blood needs more oxygen. In the 1980s, an American psychologist named Robert Provine tested this. He had students breathe air with extra oxygen, and then air with extra [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]]. Neither changed how often they yawned.

Another idea is that yawns cool the [[@brain-works|brain]]. A big gulp of air and a stretch of the jaw pull cooler blood up into the head. Some experiments support this. People yawned less often when holding a cold pack to their forehead, and animals with bigger brains tend to have longer yawns. Other scientists aren't convinced yet.

Humans aren't the only ones who catch yawns. In 2008, researchers in London yawned in front of pet [[@dogs-domestic|dogs]], and most of the dogs yawned back. Chimpanzees catch yawns from each other and even from videos of other chimps yawning. Budgerigars, the small parrots people keep as pets, catch yawns from other budgies too.

For animals that live in groups, yawning together might keep everyone on the same schedule. When one member gets sleepy and yawns, the others follow, and the group settles down. When they wake up, a round of yawns may help everyone become alert at the same time.

Babies yawn in the womb, long before they are born. [[ultrasound|Ultrasound]] scans show yawns from about three months into pregnancy. Newborns yawn a lot, but they don't catch yawns from their parents yet.

Yawns also come at odd moments. Athletes often yawn before a big race, and students before an exam, even when they aren't tired at all. Perhaps a yawn helps your body shift gear, from resting to ready or from ready to [[@sleep-why|sleep]]. If you have yawned at least once while reading this, you have just taken part in the experiment.

text: A pixel is one tiny dot in a digital picture. The word is short for "picture [[element|element]]". A screen or a photo is a grid of pixels, each showing one colour. Put enough of them close together and your eye stops seeing dots and sees a face, a sunset or a cricket match.

A Full HD TV has 1920 pixels across and 1080 down. That is about 2 million pixels, each changing colour many times a second. A 4K screen has about 8 million. On a phone they are packed so tightly that you need a [[@magnifying-glass|magnifying glass]] to see them. A good phone screen fits more than 400 pixels into every inch, about 2.5 cm.

st.prompt: A screen pixel can show yellow. Which two colours of light does it mix to make it?

options.t: Yellow is a separate light of its own

st.reveal: Screens use red, green and blue light. Red and green light together look yellow to your eyes. This is different from mixing paints, where red and green make a muddy brown.

d.try: Make pixel art. Take squared paper and draw a 10 by 10 box. Colour in whole squares only, never half a square, to make a heart, a face or a kite. Then try the same picture in a 5 by 5 box. See how much detail you lose when there are fewer pixels.
myth: A camera with more megapixels always takes better photos.

After a point, more pixels add little. The size of the light sensor, the quality of the lens and the light in the scene usually matter more. A phone with fewer, larger pixels can take better pictures in dim light.

sec.t:
To a computer, a picture is a long list of numbers. In a common system, each of the three colours in a pixel gets a number from 0 to 255. That gives 256 × 256 × 256, which is about 16.7 million possible colours.

The computer stores those numbers in [[@binary-code|binary]], as 0s and 1s. That is why a photo takes up space on your phone. A 12-megapixel photo has 12 million pixels, each needing several numbers. Phones shrink the file with clever tricks that throw away detail your eye won't miss. If you squeeze a photo too much, those tricks start to show as blocky smudges, especially around sharp edges and in clear blue skies.

sec.h: The baby in the first scan
sec.t:
In 1957, an engineer named Russell Kirsch worked at the US National Bureau of Standards, now called NIST. He and his team built a machine that could scan a photograph into a computer. The first picture they chose was a photo of his baby son, Walden.

The scan was 176 pixels wide and 176 tall, in plain black and white. It looks blocky today, but it was the start of every digital photo, medical scan and satellite image since. Kirsch later said he regretted using square pixels and wished he had tried other shapes. He spent part of his retirement working on pixels that could change shape to follow the edges in a picture.

The idea of making pictures from dots is much older than computers. In the 1880s, the French painter Georges Seurat painted whole scenes with tiny dots of pure colour, close to the style of the [[@impressionism|Impressionists]]. From across the room, the dots blend.

[[@newspapers|Newspapers]] printed photos as patterns of small dots for over a hundred years. Ancient Roman [[mosaic|mosaics]] used little stone tiles in the same way. A pixel is the newest version of a very old idea: lots of small pieces, seen from far enough away, become one picture.

text: Satellite internet sends data between a dish on the ground and a satellite in space. The satellite passes it down to a ground station connected to the wider [[@internet-how|internet]], and the answer travels back the same way.

For decades, this meant using a few big satellites in geostationary [[orbit|orbit]], about 36,000 km up. They gave coverage almost everywhere, but each request took about half a second to go there and back. New networks, like SpaceX's Starlink, use thousands of small satellites much closer, mostly around 550 km up. The delay drops to a few hundredths of a second, close to that of a home broadband line.

st.reveal: A request to a geostationary satellite goes up and down to a ground station, then the answer comes up and down again. That's more than 140,000 km, which takes light about half a second. Low satellites cut that trip to a few thousandths of a second.

sec.h: The problem with being far away
sec.t:
Light travels about 300,000 km every second, which sounds unbeatable. But when you click a link using a geostationary satellite, your request goes up 36,000 km and down 36,000 km to a ground station. The reply then makes the same trip back. That's more than 140,000 km in total, about half a second at the speed of light.

Half a second doesn't sound like much. In a video call, though, it makes people talk over each other. In an online game, you'd lose every race.

A Starlink satellite is about 65 times closer than a geostationary one. But at that height, a satellite doesn't stay in one place in the sky. It whizzes round the Earth roughly every hour and a half, crossing from horizon to horizon in a few minutes.

So you need lots of them, spread out like a moving net, with another always rising as one sets. That's why Starlink has launched thousands. The first 60 went up in May 2019. By early 2026 there were more than 10,000 in orbit.

sec.h: A flat dish that steers itself
sec.t:
Users have a flat dish about the size of a small suitcase lid. It doesn't move to follow satellites. Instead, it contains hundreds of tiny antennas. By timing their signals very precisely, the dish steers its radio beam electronically, switching from one satellite to the next in a fraction of a second.

Newer satellites talk to each other with [[@lasers|laser]] beams. Data can hop from satellite to satellite across an ocean before coming down, which helps ships, aircraft and remote islands far from any ground station.

Thousands of satellites bring new problems. [[astronomer|Astronomers]] worry because sunlight bouncing off them leaves streaks across telescope photos, and their radio signals can drown out faint signals from space. SpaceX has added darker coatings and sunshades to make its satellites dimmer, but the [[@night-sky-dark|night sky]] is still changing.

There is also the risk of collisions and [[@space-junk|space junk]]. Low satellites have one advantage here: if they stop working, the thin upper [[atmosphere|atmosphere]] drags them down within a few years, and they burn up on the way. Satellites in higher [[@spacecraft-move|orbits]] can stay there for centuries. Other companies, including Eutelsat OneWeb and Amazon Leo (once called Project Kuiper), are launching their own networks, so the sky will get busier still.

text: Curry leaves give South Indian food much of its smell. They are small, shiny, dark green leaves from a little tree that grows wild in India and Sri Lanka and in countless backyards. Their scent is hard to describe: a bit citrus, a bit nutty, a bit like nothing else.

Cooks almost always fry them first. In a step called *tadka*, or tempering, a spoonful of oil is heated with [[@mustard|mustard seeds]], dried red chillies, a few [[@lentils-world|lentils]] and a sprig of curry leaves. The leaves crackle, the seeds pop, and the flavoured oil is poured over [[@south-indian-meals|sambar]], rasam, chutney, upma or curd rice. Without curry leaves, many families would say the dish tastes unfinished.

st.prompt: Cooks usually add curry leaves to very hot oil rather than to the pot at the very end. Why?

options.t: Hot oil pulls out the leaf's scented oils and spreads them through the dish
Hot oil makes the leaves soft enough to chew
It removes a poison from the leaves

st.reveal: The leaves store their smell in tiny oil pockets. A few seconds in hot oil bursts them open, and the scent dissolves into the oil, which then carries it into every spoonful of dal or chutney.

sec.t:
The curry leaf tree belongs to the citrus family, along with oranges and limes. Its scientific name is *Murraya koenigii*. It has white flowers and small berries that turn black when ripe, and birds spread the seeds.

In Tamil the leaves are called *kariveppilai*. *Veppilai* means neem leaf, because the two leaves look rather alike. In northern India one common name is *meetha neem*, "sweet neem", even though the plants are not related to [[@neem|neem]] at all. In Hindi they are also called *kadi patta*, the leaf that goes into kadhi.

The tree is easy to grow from fresh seed or from the shoots that spring up around its roots, which is how many families share it with neighbours. It loves warmth and hates frost, so in colder places it lives in a pot indoors through the winter.

Curry leaves are everywhere in Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, and they travel well beyond the south. Cooks in Maharashtra put them in poha, Gujarati cooks add them to dhokla and kadhi, and Sri Lankan curries use them in great handfuls. Indian families who moved to Malaysia, Singapore, Fiji and South Africa took the plant with them.

Fresh leaves keep their scent for only a few days in the fridge. Dried leaves lose most of it, so cooks who live far from India often freeze them instead, or grow a tree in a pot on a sunny windowsill.

In the United States, fresh curry leaves can be surprisingly hard to find. The tree can host the Asian citrus psyllid, a tiny insect that spreads a disease called citrus greening. The disease has damaged orange groves in Florida and threatens those in California. So American rules strictly control curry leaves and plants arriving from abroad, and some states limit moving them around.

The word "curry" itself probably comes from the Tamil word *kari*, used for spiced sauces and dishes. Portuguese and then British traders picked it up, and over time "curry" came to mean almost any spiced dish from South Asia. It is one of many [[@words-borrowed|borrowed words]] that travelled from India into English. The British even invented "curry powder" so they could make something like Indian food back home. Ironically, that powder rarely has the leaf that shares its name.
